P100.s0.text: **Biology.** Aciurina luminaria is univoltine and has a life cycle and phenology similar to A. bigeloviae and A. trixa (Baine et al. 2023a; 2023b).

P100.s1.text: Eggs are laid singly into the leaf bud of a distal plant stem.

P100.s2.text: The gall forms at the oviposition site and the developing larva feeds on the tissue surrounding the central chamber of the gall.

P100.s3.text: By fall, the gall reaches full size, and the larva reaches its final instar and chews to the outer layer of the gall to create a circular trap door.

P100.s4.text: The larva ceases feeding and overwinters inside the gall, then pupates in the spring.

P100.s5.text: Adults eclose in summer and push their way through the door to emerge from the gall and find a mate.

P121.s0.text: The adaptive significance of melanized wing patterns present on tephritid fly species is unclear as studies have found evidence that these patterns could play a role in sexual communication (Benelli et al. 2014; Hippee et al. 2022), thermoregulation (Sivinski and Pereira 2005), or predator deterrence by salticid mimicry (Mather and Roitberg 1987; Whitman et al. 1988; Rao and Díaz‐Fleischer 2012).

P121.s1.text: From this study, it is clear that A. luminaria wings are not sexually dimorphic, similar to A. bigeloviae and A. trixa.

P121.s2.text: However, it is also clear that A. luminaria wings have less melanized area on them than these species, and in combination with their usually paler abdomens, indicates that there may be an advantage to paler colors in their habitats.

P122.s0.text: This is supported by our observations of wing pattern variation, which is higher in A. bigeloviae and lower in A. luminaria.

P122.s1.text: However, in the field, populations of the host plant E. n. subsp. ammophila appear largely fragmented across the range, often separated by dozens of miles, so the dispersal mechanisms of this species, if it was evolved from a single founding population, is mysterious.

P123.s0.text: Because A. luminaria occurs in sympatry with A. bigeloviae but on a unique host plant subspecies, speciation may be a result of host-race formation.

P123.s1.text: Evidence of speciation via host-race formation, from a host switch specifically, is well-supported in the tephritid genus Rhagoletis, who display extraordinary host fidelity similar to that observed in Aciurina (Abrahamson and Blair 2008) Host-race formation is also documented in the closely related galling tephritid Eurosta solidaginis (Fitch, 1855), where two populations that are specific to distinct species of host Solidago (goldenrod) are reproductively isolated via assortative mating, and oviposition preference to the plant species of maternal provenance (Abrahamson and Blair 2008).

P125.s0.text: In both Eurosta and Rhagoletis, there is substantial evidence that host switches were advantageous for enemy escape (Brown et al. 1995; Feder et al. 1995); a new niche, like a host plant and/or altered gall form may be absent of, or inaccessible to, predators that previously had a negative impact on fitness of the fly.
